transcript.text: smelt burning plastic and saw a wisp of smoke from the top of the dishwasher door, the lights went off. I've switched it off at the wall. can I just try it again?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning or hot-plastic smell, smoke, scorching or melting can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. I can't guide testing with the power on — that needs a qualified engineer. Any check I suggest is done with it switched off and unplugged. No, please don't try it again. A burning-plastic smell with smoke from the top of the door, followed by the lights going off, points to something electrical overheating. It needs checking by a qualified engineer before it's used again. Switching it back on to see what happens risks restarting whatever was burning. Switching it off at the wall was exactly right. If you can, pull the plug out too, so it's fully disconnected. Why the top of the door matters: on most dishwashers that's where the control and display electronics sit. That makes the likely causes, most likely first: 1. A failed component on the control/display board. This is the most common reason for a smell and smoke from that spot with the display then dying.
2. A burnt or overheated wiring connector in the door or panel area. This often comes from a loose or corroded joint that has heated up.
3. Moisture getting into the electronics, for example from steam or water escaping at the top of the door, and causing a short. Some simple checks you can do with it unplugged and cooled, without taking anything apart: 1. Check your consumer unit (fuse box). If a trip has gone, that suggests a short to earth and supports a wiring or moisture fault. If only the dishwasher's own lights went out, a board failure is more likely.
2. Look along the top edge of the door, the control panel and any vents for brown or black scorch marks, melted plastic or a sooty smudge. Visible damage helps the engineer and also matters for any recall claim, so take a photo.
3. Look for signs of water or steam marks around the top of the door or panel. That would point towards moisture getting in. Whatever you find, the fix is a job for an engineer. It usually means opening the door panel and working on the board or wiring. It's also worth checking for a recall. Some dishwasher makes have had safety recalls for overheating control panels. Find the model and serial number on the label around the edge of the door. Then use the manufacturer's recall checker or the GOV.UK product safety alerts page. If it is covered, the repair would be free. If it's still under warranty, contact the manufacturer rather than a general repairer.

candidates: Electrical failure on the control/display board in the top of the door (high)
Overheated or burnt wiring connector in the door or control panel (medium)
Water or steam getting into the control electronics and shorting them (low)

reading.symptom: burning plastic smell and smoke from top of door, lights went off

plan: They asked: "can I just try it again?" - answer that first.

Safety: a burning hazard is active. The fixed safety warning is shown separately, do not repeat it. It must not be used again until a qualified engineer has checked it: say that plainly. You may explain the likely cause and suggest checks that are safe with it switched off and unplugged, but never say or imply that a check could make it safe to use, or that they might not need an engineer.
The fault they reported is: "burning plastic smell and smoke from top of door, lights went off". Keep to it: never describe a symptom, result or state they have not told you.
They asked about something unsafe (live test): do not explain how to do it; the fixed safety wording is shown separately. Offer the safe alternative.

Stage 1 (broad help): say what could cause this, most likely first, as possibilities rather than certainties, including simple causes (settings, loading, detergent, installation, or normal behaviour) where they fit. Then give the safe checks that best tell those causes apart (most useful and simplest first, usually two to four), each with why it helps and what each result would mean; or, if one question would settle it sooner, ask that. Do not ask for the model number in this reply. Do not tell them to buy, order or replace a part yet.
